evidence_items.source_text: Physical examination revealed multiple, shallow ulcers with raised and sharply demarcated borders located on the medial aspects of the labia minora. Grey exudate and eschar are noted. The surrounding vulvar tissue was erythematous and markedly oedematous

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 and 2 were negative, as well as rapid plasma reagin screening for syphilis and HIV testing. Evaluation for Behcet’s syndrome was also performed, revealing negative C reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and human leucocyte antigen-B51 (HLA-B51). Testing for EBV was negative. A nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 using reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) was positive.

HSV, EBV, HIV and syphilis testing at that time were all negative. She was hospitalised for pain control for 5 days, completing a 14-day course of oral steroids. She applied topical lidocaine 5% ointment and benzocaine 20% spray for pain control. The genital oedema had decreased, but ulcers and vulvar pain were still present. She was started on colchicine 1.2 mg daily and was noted to have further improvement of oedema and pain within 1 week. Subsequent evaluation by Rheumatology was not consistent with Behcet’s syndrome, revealing negative CRP, ESR and HLA-B51.

Ulceration and oedema resolved within 6 weeks; however, she was noted to have agglutination of the labia minora. Adhesions were refractory to a trial of topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment and she underwent lysis of labial adhesions under sedation. Postoperative evaluation revealed normal anatomy, no evidence of scarring and resolution of pain.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: primary acute aphthous genital ulcers in the setting of SARS-CoV-2
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Primary acute aphthous genital ulcers, also known as Lipschütz ulcers, ulcus vulvae acutum or acute genital ulcers (AGU), are painful vulvar ulcers without an identifiable aetiology. This rare ulcerative condition occurs most frequently in virginal women and girls and is not associated with sexually transmitted infection.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 and 2 were negative, as well as rapid plasma reagin screening for syphilis and HIV testing. Evaluation for Behcet’s syndrome was also performed, revealing negative C reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and human leucocyte antigen-B51 (HLA-B51). Testing for EBV was negative. A nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 using reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) was positive.
Here, we describe a case of primary acute aphthous genital ulcers in the setting of SARS-CoV-2 in a non-sexually active adolescent girl.
